paper_metadata.title: FEEL: Framework for the integration of Entity Extraction and Linking systems
paper_metadata.abstract: Entity extraction and linking (EEL) identifies real-world objects from text and associates them with resources in a knowledge base. The paper proposes FEEL, a framework for integrating EEL systems in an ensemble setting, with recommendations for system selection, input-parameter configuration, execution, and final result integration. The filtering strategy measures entity occurrence and detects overlapping entities. FEELink implements the framework using publicly available APIs and is evaluated through GERBIL on seven datasets. The experiments report improved micro/macro precision and recall relative to selected individual EEL systems.

problem_addressed: The paper addresses the lack of clear guidance for selecting, configuring, invoking, and integrating multiple entity extraction and linking systems. Individual systems differ in domain, language, knowledge-base coverage, parameters, and output formats; combining them can create duplicate or partially overlapping entity tuples. The objective is to provide a reusable ensemble framework and demonstrate it with FEELink.

methodology.description: FEEL is an ensemble integration framework organized as a sequential pipeline. Parameter Configuration selects EEL services, manages resources, and tunes parameters, especially confidence thresholds. System Invocation prepares requests, handles runtime failures, and parses returned fields. Data Consolidation filters low-frequency, duplicate, and overlapping entity tuples using frequency thresholds, majority voting or ranking, and longest-mention replacement, then prepares RDF Turtle/NIF output. FEELink is the proof-of-concept implementation integrating TagMe, DBpedia Spotlight, Babelfy, and WAT through REST APIs.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The framework links mentions to knowledge-base resources, primarily DBpedia resources, and uses RDF Turtle for final output with the NIF vocabulary for GERBIL annotations. It does not propose a new ontology; schema use is for interoperability and evaluation output.

text_to_kg_stages: Text preprocessing: plain-text input is accepted; no additional preprocessing pipeline is specified
Entity and concept extraction: spotting named-entity mentions
Entity resolution and linking: candidate collection and disambiguation to knowledge-base resources
Knowledge fusion and deduplication: integration of outputs from multiple EEL systems, duplicate removal, and majority voting
Graph validation and correction: frequency filtering, overlap resolution, and ranking-based selection
Graph construction: serialization of final mention-URI tuples as RDF Turtle/NIF annotations

input_output.input_type: Unstructured plain text in English, including tweets, web pages, news articles, sentences, and mixed-domain documents.
input_output.input_granularity: Document- and sentence-level text, with datasets ranging from short tweets and sentences to web pages and news articles.
input_output.output_representation: Named-entity tuples containing mention, knowledge-base URI, start/end offsets, and confidence during processing; final output is a filtered set serialized as RDF Turtle with NIF annotations.

metrics: Pearson correlation between entity-type counts and micro-F1
evaluation.setting: FEELink was evaluated in GERBIL on gold-standard datasets. Four datasets were used to tune confidence thresholds by testing values from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1; three held-out datasets were used for testing. Strong matching required exact mention and URI agreement, while weak matching required exact URI agreement with an exact or partial mention match. FEELink frequency thresholds of one (fr1) and two (fr2) were compared with individual systems. A separate comparison used FEELink(fr2) against RP on IITB, MSNBC, AQUAINT, and AIDA/CONLL B.

value: Under strong matching, FEELink(fr2) reported higher micro/macro precision than each individual EEL system on all seven evaluated datasets in Table 5.
Under strong matching, FEELink(fr1) generally provided the highest recall, while FEELink(fr2) generally improved precision at the cost of recall.
Strong-matching micro-F1 for FEELink(fr2) was 0.392 on Derczynski, 0.191 on IITB, 0.570 on MSNBC, 0.377 on N3-Reuters-128, 0.510 on KORE50, 0.471 on OKE, and 0.194 on ACE2004.
Under weak matching, FEELink(fr2) micro-F1 was 0.434 on Derczynski, 0.204 on IITB, 0.597 on MSNBC, 0.442 on N3-Reuters-128, 0.527 on KORE50, 0.552 on OKE, and 0.204 on ACE2004.

Compared with RP, FEELink had higher micro-precision on IITB (0.644 vs 0.593), MSNBC (0.639 vs 0.543), AQUAINT (0.379 vs 0.341), and AIDA/CONLL B (0.662 vs 0.648), but lower micro-F1 on IITB, AQUAINT, and AIDA/CONLL B; it exceeded RP on micro-F1 for MSNBC (0.570 vs 0.482).
FEELink(fr1) extracted more entities and achieved higher recall, but also produced more false positives; FEELink(fr2) reduced false positives and improved precision.
In the qualitative analysis, FEELink(fr2) had Pearson correlation 0.610 with person counts, 0.268 with organizations, 0.270 with locations, and 0.325 with other entities.

value: Author claim: FEEL provides adaptable recommendations covering system selection, configuration, invocation, and result integration.
Experimental result: the ensemble improved precision and recall relative to the individual component systems in the reported GERBIL evaluations.
The frequency threshold exposes a useful precision-recall trade-off: fr1 favors recall and fr2 favors precision.
The framework tolerates service failures by continuing execution of remaining systems when a request fails.

Review-level inference: the explicit modular stages and common tuple/output representation make the approach comparatively easy to extend with additional EEL services, subject to resource and API constraints.

FEELink(fr2) outperformed all individual systems regarding the micro-precision because it takes into account the fact that one entity must be identified by at least two EEL systems.

value: The frequency/longest-match filtering can remove correct entities or retain incorrect entities when mentions overlap.
FEELink(fr1)'s recall advantage is accompanied by many false positives; fr2's precision advantage reduces recall.
Confidence thresholds are sensitive to datasets and may not transfer to specialized domains.
The system depends on external services, tokens, service availability, and changing knowledge-base identifiers.
The evaluation is largely black-box and does not measure resource consumption, runtime, complexity, or the appropriate domain for each component system.
Review-level inference: aggregation operates on system outputs rather than jointly learning complementary error patterns, so it cannot correct errors that are shared by all component systems.

value: The confidence-configuration strategy may not apply to different or specialized domains such as medical or biology datasets.
Increasing the number of integrated systems raises complexity and may reduce performance because of hardware limitations; a modular architecture for larger ensembles is outside the scope.
Only two frequency values were tested in the evaluation.
GERBIL datasets may be outdated because knowledge bases can change resource identifiers, causing parsing errors.
False positives may reflect missing annotations or changed dictionaries rather than actual system errors.
The comparison with third-party ensemble systems is difficult because implementation details, configurations, available services, hardware, and purposes differ.
The filtering of overlapping entities remains an open problem requiring additional criteria and functions.
Future work is needed for diverse domains, languages, additional EEL systems, and system-selection strategies based on internal features and evaluation correlations.

value: Robustly resolving partial overlaps while avoiding both false positives and false negatives remains unresolved.
Selecting the number and combination of EEL systems using internal characteristics and complementary error patterns remains unresolved.
Confidence and frequency settings that generalize across domains, languages, datasets, and knowledge bases remain unresolved.
Evaluation of black-box operational properties such as runtime, resource consumption, complexity, service availability, and cost remains unresolved.
Knowledge-base identifier changes and incomplete benchmark annotations complicate reliable evaluation.

Review-level inference: the paper does not resolve end-to-end construction of richer knowledge graphs beyond linked entity tuples; relation, event, ontology, and graph-update stages remain outside the demonstrated method.

code_and_data_availability: The paper states that a FEELink demo implementation was available for testing through a GitHub URL, and that the evaluation datasets were available through GERBIL. The paper does not state that a complete reproducibility package, all configuration files, or all source code was released.
